notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Most common poles are concrete with holes running all the way to the bottom, wide or tall. Poland's stop short of the base; Hungary's holes are smaller.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round concrete poles are also quite common, very similar to Bulgaria's.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Extremely large yellow pole stickers with the town name near the middle are specific here; smaller ones also occur, and Bulgaria and Hungary have similar ones.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Trees and poles often have white-painted bases, also common in Ukraine and parts of Russia.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Pole tops with two support bars under the crossbar, forming an upside-down triangle, are sometimes seen.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Standard long white plates with a single blue strip on the left.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are red on white, most often with a yellow frame, which is by far the commonest framing here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A yield sign with an extremely thick red border and thin white outline is unique here, though other designs exist.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Typical town entry: a yellow sign with a speed limit and city skyline above a white sign with the town name.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs are blue, arrow shaped, with a white border, and often show a red or blue road number.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Sign backs are often black, as in Italy, Albania and Germany.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Thin white bollards with a red vertical strip near the top. They are fairly rare; Turkey has a very similar one.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Waystones are very common: fairly large ones with red or blue framing and a road number on the side, rugged real stone ones, or a tiny all-white version.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Edge lines made of short dashes with narrow gaps are a good clue; centre lines are often noticeably thick, unlike thinner Bulgarian lines.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Romance language with Ă, Ș and Ț, plus Â and Î. Turkish Ş can be confused with Ș.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Dacia is the commonest brand, over a quarter of all cars; no other eastern European country passes 10%.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Single-family stone houses in pastel colours with orange tile or grey metal roofs; some have walls of painted square tiles in patterns.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Haystacks with a stick running straight through the middle are very common.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Tall forested mountains and hills in the centre; flat or rolling farmland in the south, west and east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Completely flat farmland in the south and west. Distant hills to the north mean south; to the south or east mean west.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: If nearly all roofs are orange tile, you are probably in the western half.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: If nearly all roofs are metal or plastic fake tiles, you are probably in the eastern half.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Near the western border, villages follow the neighbour's style: long straight streets, evenly spaced single-storey houses with gable ends to the road and orange tiles.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Bilingual signs with Hungarian are mostly in the central counties of Covasna, Harghita and Mureș, and less often near the Hungarian border.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: South of Iași near the eastern border, rolling farm valleys run north-northwest to south-southeast, with fields on the hilltops.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Elaborately carved wooden gates are common in the northern region of Maramureș.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sunflowers are mainly in the far east, and secondly the far west.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: The 67C mountain road has all-yellow road lines.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Windows shaped like a squinting eye are most common in the city of Sibiu.
